title: Runtime saturation signals – candidate metrics + export notes (wip)
body:
Context
- For Hosted circuit breakers + load shedding, we need runtime-provided saturation signals that are:
  (1) predictive (early warning), (2) hard to game by a single tenant, (3) cheap to collect, and (4) safe to export (bounded cardinality).
- Primary consumers:
  - Gateway admission control (coarse “are we healthy?”)
  - Smart routing (regional capacity + model availability)
  - Runtime scheduler (local backpressure)
  - SRE dashboards/alerts (trend + incident triage)

Working definitions (so we use the same language)
- “Prefill” = prompt processing phase; “decode” = token generation phase.
- “Queue depth” = number of requests waiting for a scheduler slot.
- “Backlog” = work waiting expressed in tokens (more stable than request count when prompt sizes vary).
- “Saturation” = the point where additional concurrency increases latency superlinearly (tail blow-ups), typically due to one of:
  - GPU compute utilization pinned
  - KV cache pressure / eviction
  - allocator/memory fragmentation leading to frequent allocations or OOM retries
  - scheduler contention (CPU side)

Candidate saturation signals (ranked)

1) Scheduler queue depth (prefill + decode)
- What: gauge of queued requests per model shard / runtime instance.
- Proposed metrics:
  - runtime_sched_prefill_queue_depth (gauge)
  - runtime_sched_decode_queue_depth (gauge)
- Pros:
  - Easy to understand, cheap, strong correlation with “we are behind”.
  - Works even when GPU util is noisy (kernel scheduling / mixed workloads).
- Cons:
  - Request count alone can be misleading when prompt length variance is high.
  - Can be spiky at 1s sampling; needs smoothing.
- Notes:
  - Prefer also exporting token backlog (see #2) to normalize by work.

2) Token backlog (queued tokens)
- What: sum of estimated work waiting in the queue (tokens) for prefill/decode.
  - Prefill backlog: sum(prompt_tokens) for queued requests.
  - Decode backlog: sum(remaining_max_tokens) or sum(target_tokens) for queued requests.
- Proposed metrics:
  - runtime_sched_prefill_backlog_tokens (gauge)
  - runtime_sched_decode_backlog_tokens (gauge)
- Pros:
  - Much more stable than queue depth; directly maps to expected waiting time.
  - Helps distinguish “10 small prompts queued” vs “10 huge prompts queued”.
- Cons:
  - Needs an estimate for decode remaining; if clients set huge max_tokens, backlog can overstate.
  - Potentially sensitive if exported at high cardinality (must not tag by tenant).

3) Effective throughput / saturation ratio (observed vs target)
- What: measured token/sec compared to baseline capacity for that model/hardware profile.
- Proposed metrics:
  - runtime_tokens_per_sec (gauge, smoothed)
  - runtime_saturation_ratio (gauge) = observed_tps / expected_tps (clamped 0..>1)
- Pros:
  - Normalizes across hardware, model sizes, quant profiles.
  - Good for routing decisions (“this region is at 0.85 of expected”).
- Cons:
  - Expected TPS depends on seq length distribution, batching config, tool calling, etc.
  - Requires an “expected_tps table” keyed by model + runtime config; needs ownership.
- Notes:
  - We can start with a coarse target per model family and revise later.

4) Time-in-queue / admission delay
- What: histogram of time from request accepted by runtime to start of prefill, and time from prefill done to decode start.
- Proposed metrics:
  - runtime_queue_wait_seconds (histogram)
  - runtime_decode_wait_seconds (histogram)
- Pros:
  - Best user-experience proxy; can set thresholds that map to p95/p99.
- Cons:
  - Histograms are expensive if we label too much; need careful buckets.
  - Needs consistent timestamping; clock issues across threads.
- Buckets suggestion:
  - 0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10 (seconds)

5) KV cache pressure (utilization + eviction)
- What:
  - Fraction of KV cache reserved/used
  - Eviction rate (if we evict to admit)
- Proposed metrics:
  - runtime_kv_cache_utilization (gauge 0..1)
  - runtime_kv_cache_evictions_total (counter)
  - runtime_kv_cache_bytes_in_use (gauge)
- Pros:
  - Strong signal for “imminent performance cliff” and quality of service.
  - Correlates with tail latency (cache thrash).
- Cons:
  - Implementation complexity differs by model/runtime path.
  - “Utilization” can be misleading when fragmentation exists.
- Notes:
  - If we can only do one: export eviction counter + high watermark.

6) Memory pressure proxies (allocator / fragmentation)
- What:
  - GPU memory allocated vs reserved
  - Allocation failures / retries
  - Fragmentation proxy (reserved - allocated)
- Proposed metrics:
  - runtime_gpu_mem_allocated_bytes (gauge)
  - runtime_gpu_mem_reserved_bytes (gauge)
  - runtime_gpu_alloc_failures_total (counter)
  - runtime_gpu_mem_fragmentation_bytes (gauge) = reserved - allocated (proxy)
- Pros:
  - Helps explain OOM-like incidents without full logs.
- Cons:
  - Fragmentation proxy is a heuristic.
  - Some frameworks blur “reserved” semantics.

7) GPU utilization (compute + memory bandwidth)
- What:
  - GPU SM utilization, HBM utilization, power throttling.
- Proposed metrics:
  - runtime_gpu_sm_utilization (gauge 0..1)
  - runtime_gpu_mem_bw_utilization (gauge 0..1)
- Pros:
  - Common metric; good for “are we compute-bound or stalled?”
- Cons:
  - Can be misleading in mixed batch sizes; high util may still be healthy.
  - Collection can be expensive and vendor-specific (NVML scrape frequency matters).

8) Error-based signals (late, but necessary)
- What:
  - OOM events, CUDA errors, NCCL timeouts, kernel launch failures.
- Proposed metrics:
  - runtime_cuda_oom_total (counter)
  - runtime_nccl_timeouts_total (counter)
  - runtime_inference_failures_total{reason=...} (counter, reason is low-cardinality)
- Pros:
  - Unambiguous “badness”; useful for alerting.
- Cons:
  - Usually too late for preventing latency blow-ups (but helps breaker open hard).

Sampling rates + aggregation (practical proposal)
- Goal: keep runtime overhead negligible and Prometheus footprint sane.

A) Fast loop (runtime internal, NOT exported as-is)
- 100–250ms: internal scheduler stats for adaptive batching and local backpressure.
- Output: local decisions only.

B) Export loop (Prometheus / OTel metrics)
- Default scrape/export period: 5s (preferred), with a 15s rollup for dashboards.
- For spiky gauges (queue depth): compute EWMA in-process and export both raw + smoothed (or only smoothed if we want to avoid confusion).
  - Suggest: runtime_sched_*_queue_depth (raw), runtime_sched_*_queue_depth_ewma (smoothed, alpha tuned)
- Histograms: 5s export; keep buckets limited.

C) Control-plane inputs (for breaker evaluation)
- Policy engine should evaluate on 10s windows with guardrails:
  - require N consecutive windows above threshold before “open”
  - require M consecutive windows below threshold before “close”
- Rationale: avoid flapping during batch boundary effects.

Cardinality constraints (strong guidance)
- Non-negotiable: NO tenant_id, api_key, request_id, prompt hash, org name labels on runtime metrics.
- Avoid route-level labels in runtime. Route is a gateway/control-plane concern.
- Suggested label set (max):
  - region
  - model_family (e.g., llama3, mistral, qwen)
  - model_variant (only if we can keep it bounded; else map to model_family)
  - runtime_pool (hosted/dedicated/private) OR tier (careful: tier might explode)
  - instance_group (optional; prefer sampling)
- Explicitly avoid:
  - pod name, instance id, gpu uuid as labels in exported metrics
  - If we need per-instance debugging, we do it via logs/traces or a separate “debug scrape” endpoint gated and sampled.

Where cardinality bites us today (examples)
- Including “model” with full version string (e.g., llama-3.1-70b-instruct-2025-10-18) causes churn and dashboard breakage.
  - Action: map to canonical short name; version belongs in logs, not metric labels.
- Per-GPU metrics *per instance* across a large fleet explodes series count.
  - Action: export aggregated per-instance-group metrics (sum/avg/max) + percentiles via histograms where needed.

Proposed minimum viable set for circuit breakers (Phase 1)
- Must-have (exported):
  - runtime_sched_prefill_backlog_tokens
  - runtime_sched_decode_backlog_tokens
  - runtime_queue_wait_seconds (hist)
  - runtime_kv_cache_utilization (if easy) OR runtime_kv_cache_evictions_total
  - runtime_inference_failures_total{reason=oom|cuda_error|timeout|other}
- Nice-to-have:
  - runtime_saturation_ratio
  - runtime_gpu_mem_fragmentation_bytes

How these signals map to load shedding decisions (rough)
- Soft shed (return overload w/ Retry-After, encourage backoff):
  - backlog_tokens high but stable, no error spike
- Hard shed (open breaker):
  - backlog_tokens high + increasing AND queue_wait p95 > threshold for N windows
  - OR error counters spike (OOM/cuda)
- Feature reduction candidates (if we implement):
  - When decode backlog is high: lower max_tokens cap for lowest tiers (policy-driven)
  - When queue_wait grows: reduce streaming concurrency per tenant (gateway/routing driven)

Implementation notes / gotchas
- Token accounting:
  - Ensure “prompt_tokens” is computed at runtime after tokenization, not estimated from char count.
  - For decode remaining, use min(max_tokens, server_cap) - generated_so_far.
- Multi-model instances:
  - If one runtime process serves multiple models, do NOT label every metric with model; instead run per-model metric exporters or separate pools.
- Smoothing:
  - For dashboards: prefer 1m rate/avg; for breaker: 10s windows with hysteresis.
- Traces:
  - For deep triage, add span attributes (model, region, queue_wait_ms, batch_size) in sampled traces; keep traces low volume.

Open questions
- Ownership of expected_tps table for runtime_saturation_ratio:
  - Is this runtime team (Sofia/Lena) or SRE/Perf (Peter/Christine)?
- What’s the “right” primary breaker input: backlog_tokens vs queue_wait p95?
  - My current leaning: backlog_tokens for early signal + queue_wait for user-impact gating.
- Do we need separate signals for “prefill is saturated” vs “decode is saturated” in policy engine?
  - Likely yes; prefill saturation tends to hurt first-token latency; decode hurts tail and streaming stability.

Next steps / TODO
- [Julian] confirm token backlog computation cost and where to compute (scheduler thread vs metrics thread).
- [Omar] draft metric naming + label policy for review w/ Logan (telemetry).
- [Sofia/Lena] identify which KV cache metrics are reliable across runtime paths.
- [Peter] provide initial breaker thresholds (candidate) for us-east canary once we have baseline histograms.

Appendix: quick “do not do this” list
- Don’t export per-request metrics.
- Don’t put raw model version strings in labels.
- Don’t export per-tenant metrics from runtime (gateway can do tenant-level safely if it samples/aggregates).
- Don’t page on GPU util alone.
